title.text: Machine learning: the workflow, from loans data to a first model

objects.text: What does it mean for a computer to learn from examples, and how do we know it did?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 14 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Until now we described data, explained it, and fitted a regression to explain a number. Today we start to predict. We take eight thousand loans from Nile Microfinance, a fictional lender in Uganda, and ask which loans are likely to default. You will prepare the loan file, split it, fit a first model, and compare it with a baseline model, the simplest predictor we can build.

That comparison will change how you read every accuracy figure you meet.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can name the parts of a supervised learning problem: the records, the features, the target, the training set and the test set. You can prepare data for a model, which means fixing impossible values, imputing missing values with a missing indicator, and building a new feature.

You can say why a baseline model comes first. And you can split the data, fit a first model with scikit-learn, and explain the accuracy paradox that appears when one answer is rare. We use eight thousand fictional loans from Nile Microfinance.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python machine learning lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook, prepare the loans and fit a first model.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 13 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with no laptops open. After a ten minute break we open a Colab notebook for the forty-five minute lab, where you prepare the loan file, split it, fit a baseline model and a first model.

In every step you predict first, run the cell, read the output and change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In the regression on weekly orders, what did a footfall coefficient of 0.0188 mean?
3.  The promotion coefficient was 6.8. Does that prove the promotion caused the extra orders?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 13. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In the regression on weekly orders, what did a footfall coefficient of 0.0188 mean?

A good answer is this. About 18.8 more orders for each 1,000 more people at the door, holding promotion and rainfall fixed.

Question two. What is a residual?

A good answer is this. The actual value minus the predicted value for one record. A residual plot checks whether the errors have an even spread.

Question three. The promotion coefficient was 6.8. Does that prove the promotion caused the extra orders?

A good answer is this. No. It shows an association. A cause needs an experiment or strong outside evidence.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A model learns the link between features (inputs) and a known target (the answer) from past records, then predicts the target for new records.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Supervised learning. A model learns the link between features (inputs) and a known target (the answer) from past records, then predicts the target for new records.

Features and target. Features are the input variables. The target is the variable we predict. Statistics says independent and dependent variable.

Training set and test set. The training set is what the model learns from. The test set is held back and used once at the end to score the model.

Baseline model. The simplest possible model, such as always predicting the majority class (DummyClassifier). Every real model has to beat it.

Class imbalance (accuracy paradox). One class is far more common than the other, so a model that ignores the rare class can still have high accuracy.

title.text:
A rule you write in Excel and a
rule a model learns from examples

objects.text: Excel IF rule
Supervised learning

runs.text: Show 8,000 past loans and what happened.

objects.text: Excel: you give the rule. Machine learning: you give examples.

slides.notes:
Machine learning rests on one idea, and you already know half of it. On the left is a rule you write in Excel: flag the loan as risky when the instalment-to-income ratio, the monthly instalment divided by monthly income, is above zero point six. Lenders also call it the payment-to-income ratio.

The zero point six is a hunch, so it is illustrative. On all 8,000 loans it flags 1,623. On the right is supervised learning. We show the computer 8,000 past loans and what happened to each, and it finds a rule itself. Then we test the rule on loans it has not seen, because a rule that only works on the past is no use to a lender.

What would you want to know before trusting a learned rule?

title.text:
Supervised learning: features
go in, the target comes out

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_ft_table_11.90x4.25_4125b376.png
objects.alt: Supervised learning: features go in, the target comes out

objects.text: Four real records of loans.csv. default is 1 for a borrower who stopped repaying.

slides.notes:
Here are four records of the loans file. Each record is one loan. The variables on the left are features, the inputs we know when the loan is approved: age, income, loan amount and earlier late payments. The gold column is the target, the variable we want to predict.

Here it is default, one when the borrower stopped repaying and zero when the loan was repaid. During learning the model sees the features and the known target for thousands of records and works out how they are linked. Later it sees only the features of a new loan and must predict the target.

Which of these features would you expect to matter most?

objects.text: This course says feature and target from here on, and statistics words when the topic is explanation.

slides.notes:
Here is the translation table again, this time for machine learning. A row is an observation to a statistician and an instance or record to a machine learning engineer. The input columns are independent variables or predictors in statistics, and features in machine learning. The column you want to fill in is the dependent variable, or the target.

When the target is a class it is also called a label. A yes or no column is a binary variable, and the rows you keep hidden are the test set. From here on I say feature and target. Which of these words have you already met at work?

title.text:
Two kinds of supervised problem: regression
predicts a number, classification predicts a category

rows.text: Weekly orders of a Lakeside branch
One of two classes (positive class and negative class)
One of three or more classes
The theme of a customer message (queue, price, staff and more)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_speech_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Supervised problems come in two kinds, depending on the target. If the target is a number, such as weekly orders, the problem is regression, which we did last session. If the target is a category, the problem is classification. Binary classification has two classes, and we call the one we want to find the positive class.

For us the positive class is a loan that defaulted, and the negative class is a repaid loan. Multiclass classification has three or more classes, such as the theme of a customer message, and we meet it in Session 21. Which kind of problem is your project question?

title.text: About 1 loan in 8 defaults: this is class imbalance

objects.text: 1,004 of the 8,000 loans defaulted (the positive class). 6,996 were repaid (the negative class). One class is far more common: class imbalance.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_b683d512.png
objects.alt: About 1 loan in 8 defaults: this is class imbalance

slides.notes:
Let us meet the target. In the loans file, 1,004 of the 8,000 loans defaulted, which is 12.55 percent, about thirteen in every hundred. The defaulted loans are the positive class, because they are the ones we want to find. The other 6,996 loans were repaid, the negative class.

When one class is much more common than the other, we say the data has class imbalance. Lenders live with this all the time, because the loans that hurt are the rare ones. Hold that number, because a model that ignores the rare class can exploit it. How would you build the simplest possible predictor?

title.text:
A baseline model that predicts repaid
for every loan is 87.45 percent accurate

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.96_42b1cb94.png
objects.alt: A baseline model that predicts repaid for every loan is 87.45 percent accurate

rows.text: Predictions that equal the true answer.
Predicts the majority class every time (DummyClassifier, strategy most_frequent).

objects.text: Every other model has to beat 0.8745. Accuracy is the share of correct predictions.

slides.notes:
The simplest possible model is a baseline model. It looks at the training set, finds the majority class, repaid, and predicts it for every loan. In scikit-learn it is the DummyClassifier with the strategy most frequent. Accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by all predictions. On our test set of 2,000 loans, 1,749 were repaid, so the baseline is right 1,749 times, an accuracy of 0.8745.

That is the score a real model must beat. A model that scores less than the baseline has learned nothing useful. Does eighty-seven percent sound good to you?

title.text:
The accuracy paradox: 87.45 percent
accurate and not one default caught

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_confusion_pos_7.70x4.80_99894d83.png
objects.alt: The accuracy paradox: 87.45 percent accurate and not one default caught

objects.text: Accuracy hides the rare class.

runs.text: Recall (sensitivity): the share of real defaults caught. Here 0 of 251.

slides.notes:
Here is the baseline model drawn as a confusion matrix, a two by two count of what the model said against what was true. It said repaid for all 2,000 loans. So 1,749 true negatives are correct and all 251 defaults are false negatives: missed. Accuracy is 87.45 percent, yet the share of real defaults that the model catches, called recall or sensitivity, is zero.

This is the accuracy paradox. When one class is rare, a model can be highly accurate and still useless for the job. Session 16 studies the full set of measures. Which number would a credit manager care about here?

title.text:
Look at the data before you model
it: three problems in the loans file

rows.text: 2 ages that cannot be right: 0 and 199
Replace with the median of the valid ages, 36
Median imputation, plus a missing-indicator flag
A column that leaks the answer
collection_calls is above 0 for 100 percent of defaulted loans
Leave it out of the features

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.50.png

objects.text: Every change goes in a data cleaning log with its counts, as in Session 8.

slides.notes:
Before any model, check the data. The loans file has three problems. First, impossible values: 2 borrowers have ages of 0 and 199, which cannot be right. We replace them with the median of the valid ages, 36. Second, 379 loans have a blank monthly income, 4.7 percent.

We fill them with the median and add a flag. Third, the column collection calls is above zero for every defaulted loan, because it is recorded after the loan goes bad. It leaks the answer, so we leave it out. We record every change with its count in a data cleaning log.

Which of these would you have noticed on your own?

title.text:
Imputation with a missing-indicator: flag
the blank first, then fill it with the median

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_impute_11.90x4.25_de29d06f.png
objects.alt: Imputation with a missing-indicator: flag the blank first, then fill it with the median

objects.text: Blank incomes default at 12.1 percent, the others at 12.6. The flag keeps that information.

slides.notes:
Imputation means filling a missing value. The simplest kind is median imputation. In the picture, the gold rows have a blank income. We first make a missing indicator, a flag column that is one where the income was blank and zero elsewhere. Then we fill the blank with the median of the 7,621 known incomes, 642,600 shillings.

The order matters: after filling, the blanks are gone and the flag would be all zeros. In this file the loans with blank incomes default at 12.1 percent against 12.6 for the others, so the blank carries little information here, but the flag costs nothing. Why use the median?

What would the mean do with a few very high incomes?

title.text:
Feature engineering: build a new feature, the
instalment-to-income ratio, from three existing variables

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.96_4ec5f5a4.png
objects.alt: Feature engineering: build a new feature, the instalment-to-income ratio, from three existing variables

rows.text: Loan size in UGX and the number of months to repay it.
Income per month in UGX, after imputation.
Illustrative assumption: the borrower repays the loan plus 15 percent in charges.

objects.text: Share of monthly income for one instalment (1.15 is assumed). Median 0.29, highest 9.1.

slides.notes:
Feature engineering means building a new variable from existing ones, often the step that helps a model most. A lender thinks in terms of the instalment compared with income. We compute the monthly instalment as the loan amount times one point one five, divided by the term in months.

The one point one five is an illustrative assumption for charges, because the file has no interest rate. Dividing by monthly income gives the instalment-to-income ratio, which lenders also call the payment-to-income ratio. In our file the column is called instalment to income. For loan N00001 it is 0.60: about sixty percent of the borrower income each month.

The median ratio is 0.29. Which other feature could you build from these columns?

title.text:
Default rate climbs with the instalment-to-income
ratio: 27.8 percent in the highest quarter

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_2af660b3.png
objects.alt: Default rate climbs with the instalment-to-income ratio: 27.8 percent in the highest quarter

objects.text: Each bar is the percentage of loans in that group that defaulted.

runs.text: Four equal groups of 2,000 loans, cut by the ratio.
The highest group defaults at 5.4 times the rate of the lowest.

slides.notes:
Does the new feature help?

We cut the loans into four groups of two thousand by the ratio and looked at the default rate in each. In the lowest quarter, 5.1 percent default. In the second, 7.0. In the third, 10.4. In the highest quarter, where the instalment takes more than 0.52 of income, 27.8 percent default.

That is more than five times the lowest group. A feature that separates the classes like this gives a model something to learn from. It does not prove cause, only that the groups differ. What does this say about the rule of thumb in the Excel formula?

title.text:
Use only what is known when the
decision is made: data leakage

objects.text: Known at approval
Recorded after the loan goes bad

runs.text: collection_calls is above 0 for 100 percent of defaulted loans and 21 percent of repaid ones.
It looks brilliant and is useless at approval.

objects.text: Leave it out. Session 16 studies data leakage.

slides.notes:
One more preparation decision. Some columns are only known after the outcome. Collection calls are recorded when a lender chases a loan that has gone bad, so the column is above zero for 100 percent of defaulted loans and 21 percent of repaid ones. A model that uses it looks brilliant on the data and is useless at approval time, when no calls exist yet.

This is data leakage: information about the target sneaks into the features. The rule is to use only what is known at the moment of the decision. We leave collection calls out, and Session 16 studies leakage properly. Which other column might leak?

title.text:
Hold back a test set before the model
sees anything: the train and test split

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_rowsplit_11.90x4.25_77a35052.png
objects.alt: Hold back a test set before the model sees anything: the train and test split

objects.text: The function train_test_split shuffles the 8,000 loans and cuts them in two.

slides.notes:
Now the most important habit in machine learning. A model can memorise the records it learned from, so a score on those records proves nothing. We split the loans first. The training set, 6,000 loans, is what the model learns from. The test set, 2,000 loans, is held back and scored once at the end, like covering the last rows of a sheet with paper.

In scikit-learn the function is train test split. It shuffles the rows and cuts them. Two arguments matter: stratify, and random state. What would happen if you peeked at the test set and adjusted the model?

title.text:
Stratifying keeps the default
rate the same in both parts

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.39.png

objects.text: stratify=y keeps the class proportions in both parts. random_state=42 fixes the shuffle, so you and I get the same split.

slides.notes:
A random cut could by bad luck put too few defaults in the test set. Stratifying prevents that. With stratify set to y, both parts keep the default rate of 12.55 percent. The training set has 753 defaults in 6,000 loans, and the test set has 251 in 2,000.

The random state fixes the shuffle, so a colleague who runs your code gets the same split. With the same seed, every computer running the same scikit-learn version gets the same split, so the counts in this table will match yours. Why do the test counts have to be known before we score anything?

title.text:
The train, validate, test discipline: tune on
the validation set, use the test set once

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_rowsplit_11.90x4.25_c8531bb6.png
objects.alt: The train, validate, test discipline: tune on the validation set, use the test set once

objects.text: Illustrative sizes. Today: two parts. Session 17: cross-validation plays the validation set.

slides.notes:
Real projects use three parts, called the train, validate, test discipline. The model learns its parameters on the training set. You compare models and choose settings, called hyperparameters, on the validation set. Only when you have chosen the final model do you score it once on the test set.

If you tuned on the test set, the final score would be optimistic, because the test set would have influenced your choices. The sizes on the slide are illustrative. Today we keep it simple with two parts. In Session 17 you meet cross-validation, which repeats the validation step five times on the training set and plays the role of the validation set.

Credit teams also often split by date, training on earlier loans and testing on later ones, which is called a time-based split. Why is a validation set needed at all?

title.text:
CRISP-DM is the standard six-phase cycle
for a data and machine learning project

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_crispdm_11.90x4.25_2159f6a3.png
objects.alt: CRISP-DM is the standard six-phase cycle for a data and machine learning project

objects.text: CRISP-DM stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. The arrows loop.

slides.notes:
Our workflow follows a standard that employers recognise, CRISP-DM, which stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. It has six phases. Business understanding: what is the question and the decision?

Data understanding: what do we have and what is wrong with it?

Data preparation: clean, impute, build features and split. Modelling: fit a baseline model and a first model. Evaluation: score on data the model never saw. Deployment: put it to work and monitor it, which we do in Sessions 23 and 24. The arrows form a loop, because a poor result sends you back to an earlier phase.

The gold phases are today. Where do you think most of the time goes?

title.text:
Our workflow in five steps, from the
raw loans to a score on the test set

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_a7069186.png
objects.alt: Our workflow in five steps, from the raw loans to a score on the test set

objects.text: Preparation comes first and the baseline comes before the model. The test set is used only in step 5.

slides.notes:
Here is the workflow in the order you follow it. Step one, prepare the data: fix impossible ages, impute incomes with a flag, and build the instalment-to-income ratio. Step two, split into a training set and a test set. Step three, fit the baseline model, the always repaid predictor, so you know the score to beat.

Step four, fit the first model on the training set. Step five, predict the test set and evaluate. The order matters. In this course we prepare before we split, on purpose. The medians then come from all eight thousand loans, which lets the test loans influence the training data a little.

That is a small data leakage risk, called train-test contamination, and the safe order follows this slide. Which step would you check twice?

title.text:
The safe order: split first, then let a pipeline
learn the median from the training rows only

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 1 to 3: split first. X_raw still has its blanks.
Lines 4 to 7: an imputer, a tree, and a pipeline that chains them.
Line 8: fit learns the median from the training rows only: UGX 643,200, against 642,600 on all loans.
Line 9: test loans get the training median.

slides.notes:
Here is the safe order, and it is the one you will use at work. In this course we filled the blank incomes with the median of all 8,000 loans before the split, on purpose, to keep the lab short. That is a small leakage risk: the test loans helped to decide the median.

How small?

The median income is 642,600 shillings on all loans and 643,200 on the 6,000 training loans. The safe version splits first. A pipeline, which chains steps into one model, then learns the median from the training rows only. The flag income missing is a fixed rule, so it can come before the split.

The ratio is built from income, so in a full pipeline it follows the imputer, and Session 20 builds that. Session 16 names the problem, train-test contamination. Why does the pipeline protect the test set?

title.text:
Fit and predict: the first model beats the
baseline model by only 1.3 points of accuracy

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_664a9896.png
objects.alt: Fit and predict: the first model beats the baseline model by only 1.3 points of accuracy

objects.text: model.fit learns from the training set. model.predict returns a prediction for each test loan.

runs.text: The tree asks about instalment_to_income first.

slides.notes:
Now the first model. We use a decision tree with a maximum depth of three, a model that learns a few yes or no questions about the features. You meet trees properly in Session 15. We fit it on the training set with model dot fit, and predict the test set with model dot predict.

The accuracy is 0.8875, against 0.8745 for the baseline. Over ten different random splits it ranges from 0.882 to 0.893, so a different split gives a slightly different number. The first question the tree asks is about the instalment_to_income, the feature we built, at about 0.75. Is a gain of about one point worth celebrating?

title.text:
The confusion matrix shows what
accuracy hides: 210 defaults missed

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_confusion_pos_7.70x4.80_7da2325a.png
objects.alt: The confusion matrix shows what accuracy hides: 210 defaults missed

objects.text: The tree catches 41 of the 251 defaults.

runs.text: Recall 0.16: about 1 default in 6 is caught.
Precision 0.73: of the 56 loans flagged, 41 really defaulted.
Over ten splits, 30 to 55 defaults caught.

slides.notes:
Here is the first model as a confusion matrix. Of the 251 real defaults in the test set, the tree caught 41 and missed 210. It raised 15 false alarms. Recall, the share of real defaults caught, is 0.16, so about one default in six. Precision, the share of flagged loans that really defaulted, is 0.73.

Across ten splits the number caught ranges from 30 to 55. The model is better than the baseline, which caught none, but most defaults still slip through. We improve this with other models and thresholds in Sessions 15 and 16. Would you lend using this model alone?

title.text:
Accuracy alone ranks the models wrongly: the Excel
rule has lower accuracy and finds far more defaults

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.39.png

objects.text: The Excel rule also raises 271 false alarms; the tree raises 15. Which error costs more is a business question. Session 15 turns it into a decision threshold (rule: 0.0909 with illustrative costs).

slides.notes:
Put the three predictors side by side on the same test set. The baseline has the best looking accuracy of the first two, 0.8745, and catches no defaults. The Excel rule, instalment-to-income ratio above zero point six, has a lower accuracy, 0.8005, but catches 123 of the 251 defaults, a recall of 0.49.

The tree has the highest accuracy, 0.8875, but catches only 41. The Excel rule also raises 271 false alarms, against 15 for the tree. So which model is best depends on the cost of a missed default against the cost of a false alarm. That is a business question.

Session 15 turns it into a decision threshold: with illustrative costs of one million for a missed default and one hundred thousand for a false alarm, flag a loan at probability 0.0909 or more. Which error would cost your organisation more?

title.text: Three habits that make a model result trustworthy

rows.text: random_state=42 in train_test_split and in the model
A colleague repeats your result exactly (reproducibility).
Score it once, at the end
Otherwise the final score is too optimistic.
2 ages replaced, 379 incomes imputed, 1 feature built, 1 column left out
Anyone can audit what you changed.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Three habits make a result trustworthy. First, fix the random seed. Setting random state to forty-two in the split and in the model means a colleague who runs your code gets exactly your result, which is called reproducibility. Second, keep the test set untouched until the end, and score it once.

Otherwise the final score is too optimistic. Third, write a data cleaning log: how many ages you replaced, how many incomes you imputed, which feature you built and which column you left out. Anyone can then audit what you changed. Which of these habits do you already have in Excel?

title.text:
Read the recipe before the
lab: split, baseline, fit, predict

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 1 and 2: split into training and test sets.
Lines 3 and 4: the baseline model learns the majority class.
Lines 5 to 7: make the first model and fit it on the training set.
Line 8: predict the test set. y_pred holds one 0 or 1 per test loan.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the recipe. The first call is train test split. It takes the features X and the target y and returns four things: the training features and test features, then the training target and test target. Next we fit the baseline model with the strategy most frequent.

Then we create the decision tree with a maximum depth of three and a random state, and call fit on the training set only. Finally predict on the test features gives y pred, one zero or one for each test loan. Notice that the test target is never passed to fit.

Which line would you change to make the split twenty percent?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: KeyError or AttributeError on a column name
A column name is misspelt, for example monthly_income instead of monthly_income_ugx.
Print loans.columns and copy the name.
You filled the blanks before making the flag.
Make the flag first. Reload the file and rerun.
A blank is still in X.
Check X.isna().sum() and fill the incomes.
Very high accuracy of 0.99 or more
collection_calls is in the features, so the answer leaks.
Tree accuracy is below the baseline
You scored the training set, or the split used the wrong y.

Five messages you may meet. A key error on a column name usually means a misspelt name, so print the columns and copy. If income missing is all zeros, you filled the blanks before making the flag, so reload and rerun in the right order. A value error about NaN means a blank is still in X.

An accuracy of ninety-nine percent or more is a warning, because collection calls has leaked the answer into the features. And a tree accuracy below the baseline means you scored the wrong rows. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: A model predicts repaid for every loan and scores 0.8745 on the test set. What is it called, and why is the score not impressive?
A baseline model. The score is just the share of the majority class, and the model catches no defaults.
Why do we make the missing-indicator flag before we fill the blanks?
After filling, the blanks are gone, so the flag could not mark them.
Why is collection_calls left out of the features?
It is recorded after the loan goes bad, so it leaks the answer. This is data leakage.
